items.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water in plants.

rubric.why: Identifies the theory and the continuous water column in xylem.
rubric.description: Names the theory and states that water forms a continuous column in xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming cohesion and tension and linking them to the water column in xylem.

rubric.why: Explains the force responsible for lifting water.
rubric.description: States that transpiration creates a pulling force, aided by cohesion between water molecules, which draws water upward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining transpiration pull and the role of cohesion.

modelAnswer: The Cohesion-Tension Theory explains the upward movement of water through xylem in plants.
Transpiration from leaves creates a pulling force (tension); cohesion between water molecules keeps the water column continuous, so water is pulled upward.

items.followUp: Name two places, other than the wrist, where the pulse can be felt.

rubric.why: The wrist is a common site where an artery lies close to the skin.
rubric.description: Identifies the wrist or radial artery as a pulse point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct pulse point, such as the wrist.

rubric.why: Pulse can be detected at other superficial arteries as well.
rubric.description: Names another suitable pulse point, such as the neck, temple or inner elbow.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one additional correct pulse point.

modelAnswer: Pulse can be felt at places where an artery is close to the skin, such as the wrist (radial artery), neck (carotid artery), temple, and inner elbow.

items.followUp: Describe the levels of organization in a multicellular animal, using a human as an example.

rubric.why: Defines multicellular organization as organization involving many cooperating cells.
rubric.description: Defines multicellular organization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an organism has many cells that work together.

rubric.why: Shows how cells combine to form a higher level of organization.
rubric.description: Explains that similar cells form tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the cell-to-tissue level.

rubric.why: Shows the next level in the organization of the plant.
rubric.description: Explains that tissues form organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the tissue-to-organ level.

rubric.why: Applies the levels of organization to a mustard plant.
rubric.description: Gives mustard plant examples of organs and explains that organs work together in the whole plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relevant mustard plant organs and their contribution to the organism.

modelAnswer: Multicellular organization is the arrangement of many cells that work together to perform the activities of an organism.
In a mustard plant, similar cells form tissues, and tissues combine to make organs.
The roots, stem, leaves and flowers are organs that perform different functions.
These organs work together to make the complete mustard plant.

items.followUp: Name two structures found in eukaryotic cells but not in prokaryotic cells, and state their functions.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the location and enclosure of genetic material.
rubric.description: States that prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus, while eukaryotes have one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct nucleus distinction.

rubric.why: Membrane-bound organelles are a key cell-type distinction.
rubric.description: States that prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles and eukaryotes possess them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct organelle distinction.

rubric.why: Gives an additional valid difference between the cell types.
rubric.description: Provides another accurate comparison, such as relative size/complexity or DNA form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one additional correct difference.

rubric.why: The question requires a labeled prokaryotic cell figure.
rubric.description: Draws a recognizable prokaryotic cell and labels its main parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear diagram with at least four suitable labels, including nucleoid and cell boundary.

rubric.why: The question also requires a labeled eukaryotic cell figure.
rubric.description: Draws a recognizable eukaryotic cell and labels its main parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear diagram with at least four suitable labels, including nucleus and cell boundary.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells are usually smaller and simpler; their genetic material lies in a nucleoid and is not enclosed by a nuclear membrane.
Eukaryotic cells are generally larger and more complex, with DNA enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotic cells contain organelles such as mitochondria.
Draw a prokaryotic cell as a small oval; label cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and nucleoid (DNA).
Draw a larger eukaryotic cell as an oval; label plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion and ribosomes.

items.followUp: What is taxonomy? State three characteristics used to classify organisms.

rubric.why: Defines classification as arranging organisms into groups.
rubric.description: Defines classification of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that organisms are arranged into groups.

rubric.why: Similarity and difference are the basic basis for grouping.
rubric.description: States that classification is based on similarities and differences.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying comparison of similarities and differences.

rubric.why: These are accepted characteristics used as bases for classification.
rubric.description: Names relevant characteristics used to classify organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark each for two valid bases, such as cell structure and mode of nutrition.

modelAnswer: Classification is the arrangement of organisms into groups on the basis of their similarities and differences.
Organisms may be classified by features such as cell structure, level of body organization, mode of nutrition and method of reproduction.
Their evolutionary relationships may also be considered.

items.followUp: Describe how energy is released from ATP when it is converted into ADP.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP as the cell's energy currency.
rubric.description: Names ATP as the energy currency of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying ATP.

rubric.why: These are the three components of ATP's structure.
rubric.description: Describes ATP as adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for adenine and ribose, and 1 mark for three phosphate groups.

rubric.why: The terminal phosphate bond is associated with energy transfer.
rubric.description: Identifies the high-energy bond involving the terminal phosphate group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the bond associated with energy release.

rubric.why: ATP hydrolysis releases usable energy and forms ADP and phosphate.
rubric.description: Explains that ATP breakdown forms ADP and phosphate and releases energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the products and energy release.

modelAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell.
An ATP molecule consists of adenine, a ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
The bond to the terminal phosphate group is a high-energy bond.
When this bond is broken by hydrolysis, ATP forms ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing energy for cellular activities.

items.followUp: Give two advantages and one possible disadvantage of using inorganic fertilizers.

rubric.why: Organic fertilizers supply nutrients to crops.
rubric.description: States that organic fertilizers provide nutrients to plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct nutrient-supply benefit of organic fertilizers.

rubric.why: Organic matter improves soil condition and fertility.
rubric.description: Explains a soil-improvement benefit of organic fertilizers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for humus formation or improved soil structure/water retention.

rubric.why: Inorganic fertilizers can supply concentrated nutrients quickly and in specified amounts.
rubric.description: States a benefit of inorganic fertilizers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for rapid availability or concentrated/specific nutrient supply.

rubric.why: Fertilizers support crop growth and agricultural production when used appropriately.
rubric.description: Links fertilizer use with improved crop growth or yield, preferably noting appropriate use.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid agricultural benefit of fertilizer use.

modelAnswer: Organic fertilizers, such as manure and compost, supply nutrients and add humus to the soil.
Humus improves soil structure and its ability to retain water, helping maintain soil fertility.
Inorganic fertilizers supply concentrated amounts of specific nutrients, often in a form readily available to plants.
Using suitable fertilizers in appropriate amounts supports plant growth and increases crop yield.

items.followUp: Explain the role of source and sink in the transport of sugars through a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies the source where sugars are produced.
rubric.description: States that leaves make sugars by photosynthesis and act as a source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the source.

rubric.why: Sugar loading into phloem is an essential first step in the mechanism.
rubric.description: Explains that sugars are loaded into phloem sieve tubes at the source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for phloem loading.

rubric.why: Water entry raises pressure in the sieve tubes.
rubric.description: Explains that water enters the phloem from xylem by osmosis, raising pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the osmotic water entry and pressure increase.

rubric.why: The pressure difference drives movement of phloem sap from source to sink.
rubric.description: Describes pressure-driven bulk flow toward the sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the pressure gradient and flow toward the sink.

rubric.why: Unloading at sinks completes the transport pathway.
rubric.description: Explains that sugars are unloaded at sinks and that water may return to xylem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for sink unloading or the return of water to xylem.

modelAnswer: Leaves are sources because they produce sugars, mainly sucrose, by photosynthesis.
Sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes of the phloem at the source.
The increased solute concentration draws water from the xylem into the phloem by osmosis, raising the pressure in the sieve tubes.
At sinks, such as roots, fruits or storage organs, sugars are unloaded and used or stored; pressure is lower there.
This pressure difference drives the bulk flow of phloem sap from source to sink; water can return to the xylem.
